stories.headline: Update: Pennsylvania Records Fifth Measles Death as Outbreak Reaches 943 Cases
stories.summary:
Pennsylvania health officials confirmed a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday, the latest fatality in an outbreak that has now spread to 39 of the state's 67 counties with 943 confirmed cases and 176 hospitalizations. The deceased was an unvaccinated Lancaster County resident; officials withheld further personal details citing privacy. The state's outbreak is the worst in more than 35 years.

The death marks a concrete new development in a rapidly worsening public health crisis that has already drawn national attention. Pennsylvania's toll now accounts for a significant share of fatalities in the broader national outbreak, which previously stood at two confirmed measles deaths reported by the CDC. The gap between state and federal figures underscores the lag in national tracking as cases accelerate.

Health officials have repeatedly stressed that the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is highly effective and that the overwhelming majority of cases involve unvaccinated individuals. Public health advocates are pressing for emergency vaccination campaigns in affected counties, while skeptics of vaccine mandates have argued that personal medical choice must be respected. The outbreak is testing both state health infrastructure and the limits of voluntary immunization policy.

stories.headline: France Convicts Six People Smugglers of Manslaughter in Deadliest Channel Boat Disaster
stories.summary:
A Paris court on Wednesday convicted six people smugglers of involuntary homicide for their roles in the November 2021 Channel disaster that killed 31 migrants — the deadliest such crossing on record. The six received prison sentences ranging from six to ten years. Seven additional defendants received lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was acquitted.

The victims, who included a seven-year-old child, were predominantly Iraqi Kurds along with Afghans, Egyptians, and Iranian Kurds. The court found that the convicted men, members of two cooperating trafficking networks — one Iraqi Kurdish and one Afghan — had placed migrants on a vessel that was uncertified, overloaded, and inadequately equipped with life jackets. Only two people survived the sinking.

Family members traveled from Iraqi Kurdistan to testify, providing rare personal accounts of how their relatives came to be on the boat. Lawyers for the victims' families called the verdict a relief and said the trial had 'humanised' the dead. The case carries broader significance as European governments grapple with persistent Channel crossings; the UK government separately announced Wednesday that it is scrapping its 'one in, one out' returns scheme with France, citing the pilot's failure to reach adequate scale.

stories.headline: UK Scraps 'One In, One Out' Channel Migrant Returns Scheme with France
stories.summary:
The British government announced Wednesday that it is ending a pilot agreement with France under which the UK returned some Channel small-boat arrivals to France in exchange for accepting an equal number of migrants deemed to have legitimate claims. The Home Office said the scheme had failed to reach the desired scale, with only around 1,500 people removed to France since the program began just over a year ago.

The government said flights would continue in the coming weeks to remove migrants with no right to remain, and that lessons from the pilot would be used to 'accelerate efforts' going forward. The French Interior Ministry confirmed it is in discussions with Britain on the terms of the exit. Channel crossings are down 42 percent year-on-year, with 19,135 people crossing between January and late September 2026, but the government has faced persistent pressure to show more decisive results.

The announcement comes on the same day a Paris court sentenced six people smugglers for the 2021 Channel disaster that killed 31 migrants, highlighting the continued lethality of the crossings and the complexity of enforcement across two sovereign jurisdictions. Critics from the right argue the returns scheme was always too limited to act as a deterrent, while migrant advocacy groups contend that deterrence-focused policies fail to address the conditions driving flight from countries like Eritrea, which accounted for 18 percent of arrivals in the most recent annual figures.

stories.headline: Nepal Landslides Kill 30, Strand Hundreds of Trekkers on Annapurna Circuit
stories.summary:
A new wave of landslides and heavy rainfall struck Nepal this week, killing approximately 30 people and affecting more than 1,900 families, the country's national disaster management authority reported Wednesday. More than 240 homes have been damaged, and roads, bridges, and buildings have been swept away across several districts. The disaster follows August's catastrophic flooding that left 1,400 dead and thousands missing.

Hundreds of trekkers on the Annapurna Circuit, one of Nepal's most economically important hiking routes, were forced to evacuate. Many were airlifted by helicopter from the Manang and Mustang districts as trails became impassable. Those who trekked out on foot described crossing dozens of active landslide zones over multiple days, navigating collapsed roads and destroyed bridges.

The repeated disasters this season are testing Nepal's emergency response capacity and threatening the tourism revenue the Annapurna Circuit generates. Local residents described losing homes and relatives, with some sheltering in leaking tents with nowhere else to go. Rescue operations are ongoing, and authorities have been using excavators to try to drain a landslide-created lake near the village of Chame that has inundated houses and a critical bridge.

stories.headline: Update: UK Prime Minister Says Iran 'Played a Part' in Foiled RAF Fairford Attack
stories.summary:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday there are 'strong indications' that Iran was behind the alleged thwarted attack on RAF Fairford, a U.S. air base in England used to launch strikes against Iran. Burnham made the statement in a BBC interview, marking the most direct official attribution yet of state responsibility for the incident, in which five suspects were arrested near the base over the weekend on terrorism and explosives charges.

The development is significant because it formally implicates Iran's government in an act of alleged sabotage on British soil targeting American military infrastructure, raising the stakes in the broader U.S.-Iran conflict. The accusation comes as the two countries remain in tense standoff over Iran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.

Burnham did not provide specific evidence for the claim, and Iran has not responded publicly to the allegation. The incident is being investigated by British counter-terrorism authorities in coordination with U.S. officials, who had previously indicated a foreign actor was involved.

stories.headline: Update: Iran's IRGC Appeals Directly to American Voters as Rial Hits Record Low Amid U.S. Conflict
stories.summary:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps issued a 25-page open letter to the American public on Tuesday, urging voters ahead of the November 3 midterms to oppose President Trump and pressure Washington to end the war. IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi presented the letter in Tehran, blaming Trump and U.S. support for Israel for the conflict and accusing the president of misleading Americans about Iran's nuclear program and the state of the economy.

The letter comes as Iran faces severe economic strain, with the rial falling to a record low of more than 2.5 million to the U.S. dollar on Tuesday — a dramatic collapse that underscores the impact of U.S. sanctions and military pressure on the Iranian economy. The move represents an unusual direct intervention by a foreign military force in American domestic politics.

Supporters of the Trump administration's posture argue Iran's appeal reflects weakness and desperation, noting the rial's collapse as evidence that maximum-pressure policies are working. Critics contend the administration's approach has heightened the risk of broader military escalation without a clear diplomatic off-ramp, and some argue the IRGC letter could inflame tensions further heading into the midterms.

stories.headline: Fed Watchdog Clears Powell of Criminal Wrongdoing in $2.4 Billion HQ Renovation
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve's independent inspector general released a report Wednesday finding no criminal violations by former Fed Chair Jerome Powell or other Fed officials in connection with the central bank's $2.4 billion headquarters renovation project in Washington. Inspector General Michael Horowitz's office acknowledged the Fed 'has not effectively executed' the construction management risk contract and that costs were poorly managed, but made no referral to the U.S. attorney general.

The findings effectively close the door on a Justice Department criminal investigation into Powell that became public in January — an unprecedented probe that critics viewed as part of President Trump's sustained pressure campaign against the Fed and its former chair. Trump repeatedly attacked Powell over the renovation costs while simultaneously pushing him to lower interest rates.

Supporters of the investigation argued the ballooning costs of the project warranted scrutiny and that the DOJ had a legitimate basis to look into potential mismanagement. Critics, including many economists and legal observers, warned that criminalizing a building renovation dispute set a dangerous precedent for the independence of the Federal Reserve. The watchdog's report draws a clear line between mismanagement and criminality.

stories.headline: DOJ Files Misconduct Complaints Against Federal Judges Who Spoke to Press About Immigration Enforcement
stories.summary:
The Justice Department on Wednesday filed misconduct complaints against a group of federal judges in Minnesota after they spoke to The New York Times about the impact of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge on their court. The complaints targeted two jurists who spoke on the record and others who spoke anonymously to the paper, alleging their statements violated judicial conduct standards.

The move escalates the Trump administration's ongoing confrontation with the federal judiciary, using the DOJ as a vehicle to pursue formal disciplinary action against judges who have publicly commented on immigration policy. One of the judges named is Patrick Schiltz, a George W. Bush appointee. The complaints do not carry immediate legal consequences but could trigger a formal review process.

Supporting the administration's position, officials argue that sitting judges should not be making public statements that amount to policy advocacy or that could undermine the administration's enforcement authority. Critics, including civil liberties groups and legal scholars, say the complaints represent an alarming attempt to intimidate judges and chill constitutionally protected speech, warning that targeting the judiciary for press statements threatens the separation of powers.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Allows Trump Administration to Continue Third-Country Deportations
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court handed the Trump administration an interim immigration victory on Wednesday, staying a federal district court ruling that had imposed additional procedural requirements before migrants could be deported to countries other than their own. The justices also agreed to take up the underlying legal challenge, scheduling arguments for the December session. The unsigned order means third-country removals can continue while the legal battle proceeds.

The court's three liberal justices — Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson — said they would have denied the administration's request for a stay. The administration had argued that the lower court's procedural requirements were disrupting sensitive diplomatic negotiations with countries willing to accept deportees and causing "significant and irreparable harm to U.S. foreign policy."

Supporters of the policy argue it is a necessary tool for removing migrants when their home countries refuse to accept them, and that judicial interference undermines U.S. leverage abroad. Critics and attorneys representing migrants contend the lower court's safeguards were minimal — designed only to give individuals a chance to raise claims of potential persecution or torture in the destination country — and that the ruling removes basic due process protections.

The decision is among the most significant immigration rulings of the Trump administration's second term, with implications for over a million migrants and the broader legal architecture of U.S. deportation policy. The case will return to the court for full briefing and argument in December.

stories.headline: Update: Flydubai Copilot Arrested After Allegedly Stabbing Pilot and Attempting to Crash Israel-Bound Flight
stories.summary:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed Wednesday that a copilot aboard a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has been arrested after allegedly stabbing the other pilot during approach to Israel and attempting to crash the aircraft. The plane went into a steep plunge before a passenger and crew member entered the cockpit, subdued the attacker, and diverted the flight to an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All passengers subsequently arrived safely at Ben Gurion Airport.

Israeli officials characterized the incident as an "attempted jihadist terror attack." Passenger Ron Levi told CBS News it was "the scariest thing possible," and passenger Miriam Ohayon said people on board felt the jet lose control and heard screams. "When they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood," she told Israeli television.

This is a significant new development beyond the earlier report of a cockpit altercation: the copilot's arrest, Netanyahu's public statement identifying the incident as a terror attack, and survivor accounts published Wednesday all materially advance the story. Flydubai has not yet publicly confirmed the terror characterization, and details about the suspect's identity and motive remain under investigation by Saudi and UAE authorities.

stories.headline: Ethiopia Fighting Escalates in Tigray, Killing at Least 52 Civilians
stories.summary:
At least 52 civilians have been killed over three days of heavy fighting around the town of Alamata in Ethiopia's Tigray region, according to hospital sources who spoke to the BBC. Government troops appear to have taken control of Alamata from regional fighters and are pressing north toward Mekelle, Tigray's main city. Social media footage shows army tanks in Alamata's streets, while communications to the region have been severed.

The renewed conflict follows months of escalating tension between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which administers the region. Both sides accuse each other of firing the first shots and of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a two-year civil war. Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières reported that more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray over recent days. Victims include children as young as three days old.

Fighting has spread to neighboring Amhara region, where 33 tourists — including a group of British visitors — remain stranded in Lalibela, a UNESCO World Heritage site home to ancient rock-hewn churches, after the local airport closed to commercial flights. Fourteen Israeli tourists were evacuated by military helicopter. Ethiopia also accuses neighboring Eritrea of supporting the armed groups, a charge Asmara denies, raising fears of a wider regional escalation.

The TPLF had recently joined a seven-member armed alliance with other Ethiopian rebel movements with the stated goal of removing the government in Addis Ababa. The conflict also threatens a strategic corridor connecting landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports, raising concerns about humanitarian access and regional stability.

stories.headline: Citadel CEO Ken Griffin Donates $3 Billion to Carnegie Mellon in Largest Gift in U.S. Higher Education History
stories.summary:
Hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin, founder and CEO of Citadel, announced Wednesday a $3 billion donation to Carnegie Mellon University — the largest individual gift in the history of American higher education and Griffin's largest personal donation to date. The funds will support the construction of a new Carnegie Mellon campus in Miami as well as major investments at the university's main Pittsburgh campus.

Griffin, 57, leads Citadel, widely described as the most profitable hedge fund in history. Carnegie Mellon is renowned for its programs in computer science, artificial intelligence, and engineering, making it a natural target for a technology-focused philanthropic investment of this scale. University officials said the gift will significantly accelerate research and expand the institution's footprint.

The donation arrives amid broader debates about the role of wealthy donors in shaping elite higher education and as universities navigate federal funding pressures. At $3 billion, the gift dwarfs previous records and is expected to reshape Carnegie Mellon's national and global profile for decades.

stories.headline: Last U.S. and UK Troops Withdraw from Iraq, Ending Decade-Long Anti-ISIS Mission
stories.summary:
The final British and American troops have departed Iraq, concluding a military presence that began in 2014 as part of the international coalition against the Islamic State. Approximately 100 remaining UK personnel withdrew from Irbil in the northern Kurdistan region in coordination with U.S. forces, fulfilling a withdrawal agreement signed two years ago between Washington and Baghdad. The mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, is now formally ended.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi marked the departure as Iraq's transition to 'full responsibility for its security and stability,' with the government planning four national 'Sovereignty Days' to commemorate the withdrawal. The Pentagon confirmed the coalition's departure represented 'the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated IS in Iraq,' while the UK Ministry of Defence noted that Iraqi Security Forces and Kurdish Peshmerga are now positioned to take primary responsibility for the country's security.

Significant security challenges remain. A recent UN report estimated IS retains several hundred fighters still capable of carrying out operations, and Iranian-backed militias — which have resisted Iraqi government efforts at disarmament — could see their influence expand with the U.S. presence gone. Prime Minister Zaidi has vowed to bring all armed factions under state control, but powerful militia groups have so far resisted those efforts.

The withdrawal closes a chapter that began with the 2003 U.S.-led invasion and continued through successive military missions. Hundreds of NATO troops stationed in Baghdad had already departed earlier this year, and the Irbil exit marks the definitive end of the Western military footprint in Iraq.

stories.headline: DHS Tapped $20 Million in Taxpayer Funds for Pro-Trump Campaign-Style Ads Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security used $20 million in taxpayer money — drawn from funds intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection — to produce and air campaign-style advertisements glorifying President Donald Trump, according to reporting by the Associated Press and Axios. President Trump is personally selecting which ads run, and an administration official told Axios, 'This is just the beginning,' signaling more ads are planned ahead of the November midterm elections.

The White House has characterized the spots as 'public service announcements,' but the seemingly partisan nature of the content has drawn bipartisan condemnation. Critics across the political spectrum, including a senior Republican senator, have called the spending a blatant misuse of public funds that likely violates federal anti-propaganda statutes, which prohibit the executive branch from using appropriated money to produce domestic propaganda.

Democrats have demanded formal investigations and called the ads an abuse of government resources for electoral purposes. A growing number of Republicans have also publicly distanced themselves from the practice, raising questions about legal accountability and oversight of executive spending authority. The controversy arrives five weeks before midterm elections in which control of Congress is at stake.

The episode highlights broader tensions over the Trump administration's use of federal resources in politically charged ways, with legal experts noting that the Anti-Deficiency Act and other statutes may have been violated. No formal legal action has been announced as of Wednesday.

stories.headline: FlyDubai Flight Diverted to Saudi Arabia After Pilots Physically Fight in Cockpit
stories.summary:
A FlyDubai commercial flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an altercation broke out between the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit. Both pilots were hospitalized following the incident, which the airline described only as an onboard 'incident' without providing additional details about the nature or severity of the confrontation.

Reports from multiple outlets indicate the two pilots engaged in a violent physical fight mid-flight, prompting the diversion. Saudi Arabian authorities received the aircraft, and passengers were offloaded safely. The flight's emergency landing in Saudi Arabia — a country that only in recent years opened its airspace to Israeli-bound flights — added a geopolitical dimension to what was already an extraordinary aviation safety event.

FlyDubai has not publicly explained what triggered the confrontation or provided an update on the pilots' conditions. Aviation authorities in the UAE and Saudi Arabia are expected to investigate the incident. Physical altercations between flight crew members in the cockpit are extremely rare and represent a serious breach of aviation safety protocols.

stories.headline: Update: Measles Exposures Spread to Trains and Sports Venues as National Outbreak Widens
stories.summary:
The ongoing national measles outbreak has expanded its reach to public transportation and sports venues, health officials confirmed Wednesday, raising new concerns about exposure risks for travelers. Active outbreaks are centered in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and New York, with cases now spanning 47 states. The CDC has previously raised the national death toll to two, and Pennsylvania alone has surpassed 900 confirmed cases.

Health authorities are urging travelers to verify their vaccination status before using planes, trains, or attending large public gatherings, as measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases known and can linger in the air of enclosed spaces for up to two hours after an infected person has left. The MMR vaccine is considered highly effective, providing approximately 97 percent protection after two doses.

The new transportation and venue exposure sites represent a material escalation in the outbreak's geographic spread and transmission risk, particularly for unvaccinated individuals or those with compromised immune systems. Public health officials have stopped short of issuing formal travel advisories but are recommending that anyone without confirmed vaccination history consult a physician.

stories.headline: Trump Signs Voluntary AI Safety Accord with Top Tech Leaders at White House Summit
stories.summary:
President Trump hosted the chief executives of America's largest artificial intelligence companies at the White House on Tuesday, emerging with what he called a "morally binding" voluntary accord on AI safety standards. Signatories include Trump himself alongside Google's Sundar Pichai, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, SpaceX's Elon Musk, and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.

Under the agreement, companies take responsibility for ensuring the safety of their own AI systems, committing to implement safeguards, detect and fix unintended behaviors, and work with independent auditors to assess whether their platforms operate as intended. Trump said he would establish a board to oversee AI safety, though he provided no details on its membership or authority. He described the accord as "almost like a constitution, in a way."

Supporters of the deal, including Zuckerberg, said it gives the American public "confidence that the technology works" as intended. Amodei framed it as a way "to win safely." Critics, however, were sharply dismissive. Law professor Kimberlee Weatherall called it "deeply unimpressive," noting the agreement allows firms to "define what counts as safety" and specifies no consequences for breaches. AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said it shows "emerging consensus" but fails to address developer accountability.

The summit comes amid growing international pressure for binding AI regulation and follows a series of AI safety incidents that have heightened scrutiny of the industry's self-policing. The voluntary nature of the accord — with no enforcement mechanism — is the central point of contention between the administration and outside experts who have called for legally enforceable rules.

stories.headline: Update: South Korea Demands North Korea Apologize for DMZ Landmine Blasts That Wounded Three Soldiers
stories.summary:
South Korea's military formally demanded an apology from North Korea on Tuesday after concluding with certainty that landmine explosions in the Demilitarized Zone on September 21 were caused by North Korean mines, wounding three South Korean personnel on South Korea's side of the buffer zone. Seoul called the blasts a clear violation of the 1953 armistice and vowed to take "corresponding measures."

North Korea flatly denied responsibility. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un and one of Pyongyang's most powerful officials, accused Seoul of "cooking up" the claims as a "deliberate and planned strained assertion" to shift blame and escalate tensions. Her statement, published in state media, warned the South to be "prepared for paying a price for the farce of their own making."

South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang as part of ongoing efforts to fortify its side of the border. The incident mirrors a 2015 episode in which two South Korean soldiers were maimed by mines in the DMZ, an event Pyongyang also denied. Kim Yo Jong referenced that earlier incident, claiming Seoul had used it as a pretext for escalation then and was doing the same now.

Experts warn the current situation is more volatile than the 2015 confrontation. Crisis Group senior consultant Christopher Green told the BBC that North Korea has been "wilfully attempting to harden the border" and that the two Koreas no longer maintain the low-level communication channels that existed a decade ago. "Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he said.

stories.headline: France Detains More Than 400 as Student Protests Over School Conditions Escalate Nationwide
stories.summary:
French authorities detained more than 440 people — the majority of them minors — on Tuesday as student demonstrations over overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages escalated into violence across the country. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed the detentions, noting that roughly two-thirds resulted in formal police custody. At least 400 schools were affected, according to the education ministry.

The unrest, which began in the Île-de-France region around Paris last week, spread to schools across France. Protesters blockaded school entrances, set bins alight, damaged bus stops, and hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas. At least ten teachers, several students, and 48 law enforcement officers were injured during Tuesday's clashes.

"We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old student told AFP. "The education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible." Education Minister Édouard Geffray affirmed students' right to protest but condemned the violence as "indefensible," while student union president Ryad Rani accused police of using excessive force and characterized the government's response as "repression."

The student protests coincided with separate nationwide strikes by unions representing teachers, hospital staff, and civil servants over low wages and working conditions, drawing at least 200,000 participants. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had warned Monday that further escalation would be "irresponsible" after 164 arrests the previous day, but the demonstrations intensified regardless, raising pressure on the government to address underlying grievances in France's public education system.

stories.headline: Morocco Names First Female Prime Minister After Centrist Party Wins Parliamentary Elections
stories.summary:
Fatima Zahra El Mansouri was named Morocco's first female prime minister on Tuesday by King Mohammed VI, following last week's parliamentary elections in which her centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won the most seats. The appointment makes El Mansouri only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden.

El Mansouri, 50, is a lawyer by training and has served as mayor of Marrakesh since 2009, with an interruption during which she served as a minister overseeing housing and urban planning. She was chosen by the king over PAM's other leading figure, football federation chief Fouzi Lekjaa. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy in which the king retains predominant authority, and the prime minister is appointed by the monarch from the party winning the most seats in parliamentary elections.

El Mansouri has been a prominent figure in Moroccan politics for nearly two decades but has rarely spoken publicly about gender equality or women's rights — topics of active debate in Morocco, including ongoing discussions over polygamy and inheritance law. Asked at a press conference whether state religious ceremonies might need to be modified to accommodate her as head of government, she declined to answer directly, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country.

With 97 seats, PAM does not hold a majority in parliament and will need to build a coalition government. El Mansouri's appointment is seen as a significant symbolic milestone in a Muslim-majority country in the Arab world, where female heads of government remain exceedingly rare.
